SQL for Data Analysis · Lesson 1

Databases, RDBMS & SQL Basics

Understand what a database is, how relational databases organise data into tables, the vocabulary of SQL, the four families of SQL statements (DDL, DML, DCL, TCL), how SQL compares with Excel, and how to install SQL Server and SSMS and run your first query.

● SQL class 1✦ SQL Server 2022 / SSMS 21, 2026Beginner⏱ 100 min
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain what a database, a DBMS and an RDBMS are and why companies use them instead of spreadsheets
  • Use the core vocabulary (table, row/record, column/field, schema, query, result set)
  • Classify SQL statements into DDL, DML, DQL, DCL and TCL
  • Compare Excel and SQL and know when to use each
  • Install SQL Server Developer edition and SSMS, connect, create a database and run a first SELECT

What is a database?

A database is an organised collection of data stored so that it can be found, updated and analysed efficiently and safely by many people at the same time. A DBMS (database management system) is the software that manages it. Your bank balance, every Swiggy order, every Aadhaar-linked record and every hospital appointment lives in a database.

Types of databases

Type Organises data as Examples Typical use
Relational (RDBMS) Tables with rows and columns, linked by keys SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQLite Orders, payments, HR, finance: most business data
Document JSON-like documents MongoDB, Cosmos DB Product catalogues, app content
Key-value Key → value pairs Redis, DynamoDB Caching, sessions
Column-family / warehouse Columns, built for analytics Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks SQL Analytics on huge data
Graph Nodes and edges Neo4j Social networks, fraud rings
Vector Number vectors (embeddings) pgvector, Pinecone AI search and RAG (GenAI track)

This track focuses on relational databases and SQL, the language almost every data role uses daily. You will practise in Microsoft SQL Server with SSMS, as in class. The SQL you learn transfers to PostgreSQL, MySQL, Snowflake and BigQuery with small differences in functions.

How a relational database organises data

The vocabulary

DefinitionTerms you will use every day

Table (relation): a set of rows about one kind of thing, such as customers or orders. Row (record, tuple): one item, such as one customer. Column (field, attribute): one property, such as city. Every value in a column has the same data type. Primary key: the column (or columns) that uniquely identifies each row, such as customer_id. Foreign key: a column that refers to the primary key of another table, linking them. Schema: (1) the structure of the database (tables, columns, types, relationships); (2) in SQL Server, a named container of objects such as dbo. Query: a request for data written in SQL. Its output is a result set. SQL: Structured Query Language, the standard language for relational databases (ANSI/ISO standard since 1986–87). Pronounced "S-Q-L" or "sequel". T-SQL: Transact-SQL, Microsoft SQL Server's dialect with extra features (variables, TOP, procedures).

Here is the course's retail database. The order data is split into related tables instead of one wide sheet:

Your first queries

A SELECT statement asks for columns FROM a table. Here are the first rows of the customers table:

SQL
SELECT TOP 6 customer_id, customer_name, segment, city, region
FROM customers;
Result
customer_id customer_name segment city region
C0001 Saanvi Khan Corporate Chandigarh North
C0002 Meera Bose Corporate Delhi North
C0003 Riya Shah Consumer Kolkata East
C0004 Diya Fernandes Corporate Indore West
C0005 Neha Sharma Corporate Hyderabad South
C0006 Vikram Mehta Consumer Chandigarh North
6 rows × 5 columns

How many rows are in each table?

SQL
SELECT 'customers' AS table_name, COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM customers
UNION ALL SELECT 'orders', COUNT(*) FROM orders
UNION ALL SELECT 'order_items', COUNT(*) FROM order_items
UNION ALL SELECT 'products', COUNT(*) FROM products;
Result
table_name row_count
customers 800
orders 3200
order_items 6323
products 78
4 rows × 2 columns

A taste of what is coming: total sales by region in one statement (Lesson 7 explains GROUP BY):

SQL
SELECT c.region,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sales), 0)     AS total_sales
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY c.region
ORDER BY total_sales DESC;
Result
region orders total_sales
South 831 53,952,769
West 811 51,958,521
North 792 49,018,161
East 766 46,484,119
4 rows × 3 columns
TipSQL reads almost like English

"Select the region, the number of distinct orders and the total sales, from customers joined to orders and order items, grouped by region, ordered by total sales descending." That readability is why SQL has lasted 50 years.

Properties of SQL

  1. Declarative: you say what you want, not how to get it. The database's query optimiser decides the fastest way (which index, which join order).
  2. Set-based: statements work on whole sets of rows at once, not one row at a time like a loop.
  3. Not case-sensitive for keywords: select, SELECT and Select are the same. By convention, keywords are written in UPPERCASE. In SQL Server, text comparisons are usually case-insensitive too (default collation).
  4. Whitespace does not matter: you can split a query over many lines; indent it for readability.
  5. Statements end with a semicolon ; (optional in SQL Server for most statements, but a good habit).
  6. Standard, with dialects: the core is an ANSI/ISO standard; each product adds its own functions (T-SQL, PL/pgSQL, MySQL).

The families of SQL statements

Family Full name What it does Example
DDL Data Definition Language Creates and changes the structure: databases, tables, columns CREATE TABLE customers (...)
DML Data Manipulation Language Adds, changes and removes rows INSERT INTO customers VALUES (...)
DQL Data Query Language Reads data SELECT * FROM customers
DCL Data Control Language Gives and removes permissions GRANT SELECT ON customers TO analyst
TCL Transaction Control Language Groups changes so they succeed or fail together BEGIN TRAN … COMMIT

Many books put SELECT inside DML; others separate it as DQL. Both are fine in interviews if you explain them.

Excel vs SQL

Task Excel SQL
See the data Open the sheet SELECT * FROM table
Filter rows AutoFilter WHERE
Sort Sort dialog ORDER BY
New calculated column Formula in a new column Expression in SELECT
Totals by group Pivot table / SUMIFS GROUP BY with SUM
Filter groups Pivot value filter HAVING
Lookup from another table VLOOKUP / XLOOKUP JOIN
Stack two tables Copy-paste / Power Query Append UNION ALL
Remove duplicates Remove Duplicates DISTINCT
Rank / running total RANK, SUM($B$2:B2) Window functions RANK() OVER, SUM() OVER
Data size ~1 million rows per sheet Billions of rows
Repeatability Manual steps (unless Power Query) Saved queries, views, procedures
Sharing Files get copied One source of truth with permissions

Use Excel for quick, small, ad-hoc analysis and presentation; use SQL to get, combine and summarise data at source. In practice analysts use both: SQL to extract the right data, Excel or Power BI to present it.

Installing SQL Server and SSMS

Step by stepInstall on Windows (free)
  1. Download SQL Server 2022 Developer edition (free, full-featured, for development and learning) from Microsoft's SQL Server downloads page. Choose Basic installation. Express edition is also free but limited to 10 GB per database.
  2. Note the instance name shown at the end (for example MSSQLSERVER = default, or SQLEXPRESS).
  3. Download and install SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) from Microsoft Learn ("Download SSMS"). SSMS is the editor you write queries in.
  4. Open SSMS → Connect to Server: Server type Database Engine; Server name localhost (or localhost\SQLEXPRESS); Authentication Windows Authentication; tick Trust server certificate → Connect.
  5. In Object Explorer you will see Databases, Security and more. Click New Query (Ctrl + N).
NoteMac or Linux?

SQL Server runs in Docker on Mac and Linux (mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server image). Connect with VS Code + the MSSQL extension or Azure Data Studio's successor tools. Alternatively, practise the same SQL in PostgreSQL (pgAdmin) or SQLite (DB Browser); only a few functions differ.

Create a database and load data

SQL
-- 1. Create the database and switch to it
CREATE DATABASE RetailDB;
GO
USE RetailDB;
GO
-- 2. Check which database you are in
SELECT DB_NAME() AS current_database;

To load the course CSV files: right-click the database → Tasks → Import Flat File → choose customers.csv → check the column names and data types in the preview (make IDs nvarchar, dates date, amounts decimal(12,2)) → Finish. Repeat for the other files. Lesson 4 shows how to create tables with SQL and load them with BULK INSERT.

Running queries in SSMS

Action Shortcut
Execute the whole window (or the selected text only) F5 or Ctrl + E
New query window Ctrl + N
Comment / uncomment selected lines Ctrl + K, Ctrl + C / Ctrl + K, Ctrl + U
Show/hide results pane Ctrl + R
IntelliSense refresh (after creating tables) Ctrl + Shift + R
Results to grid / text / file Ctrl + D / Ctrl + T / Ctrl + Shift + F
Estimated execution plan Ctrl + L
TipSelect a part, run a part

Highlight just one statement and press F5 to run only that statement. This is how you test a long script step by step.

Summary

Key takeaways
  • A database stores shared data safely; an RDBMS stores it in related tables of rows and columns.
  • Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys link tables.
  • SQL is declarative and set-based; keywords are not case-sensitive; statements end with ;.
  • Statement families: DDL (structure), DML (rows), DQL (SELECT), DCL (permissions), TCL (transactions).
  • Excel is for quick analysis and presentation; SQL is for getting, combining and summarising data at scale.
  • Practise in SQL Server Developer + SSMS (or Docker / PostgreSQL on Mac).
Quick quiz6 questions · tap an answer to check it

1. Which statement family does CREATE TABLE belong to?

Answer: A. DDL defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE.

2. In a relational database, what links the orders table to the customers table?

Answer: B. orders.customer_id is a foreign key that refers to customers.customer_id.

3. What does "SQL is declarative" mean?

Answer: B. The optimiser chooses the execution plan; you write the logic.

4. Which is NOT an advantage of a database over a spreadsheet?

Answer: D. For quick one-off charts, Excel is usually faster. Databases win on scale, safety and sharing.

5. GRANT SELECT ON orders TO analyst_role is an example of:

Answer: C. DCL controls permissions.

6. In SSMS, what does pressing F5 with part of the script highlighted do?

Answer: A. Highlighting limits execution to the selected text.
ExerciseMap the vocabulary

For the orders table in RetailDB, name: (a) one row; (b) one column; (c) the primary key; (d) the foreign key and the table it refers to; (e) the statement family of INSERT INTO orders ….

Show solution

(a) One order, for example the row for IN-2023-00001. (b) Any field, for example ship_mode. (c) order_id. (d) customer_id, which refers to customers.customer_id. (e) DML.

Interview cornerQuestions you may be asked

Q: What is the difference between DBMS and RDBMS? A DBMS manages data in any form; an RDBMS stores data in tables with relationships defined by keys, enforces integrity with constraints and uses SQL. Examples: SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle.

Q: Explain DDL, DML, DCL and TCL with examples. DDL changes structure (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE); DML changes rows (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE); DCL manages permissions (GRANT, REVOKE); TCL manages transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVE TRANSACTION). SELECT is sometimes called DQL.

Q: Why would a company keep data in SQL Server instead of Excel files? Concurrency, scale, data integrity (constraints, transactions), security and auditing, backup and recovery, and a single source of truth for reports and applications.

SQL for Data Analysis · Lesson 2

ER Diagrams, Relationships, Keys & Normalisation

Design databases the way professionals do. Draw ER diagrams, read crow's-foot notation, model one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships, master every type of key (super, candidate, primary, alternate, composite, foreign, surrogate) and normalise tables to 3NF.

● SQL class 1✦ 2026Beginner⏱ 110 min
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Read and draw an ER diagram with entities, attributes and relationships
  • Identify 1:1, 1:N and M:N relationships and resolve M:N with a junction table
  • Define super, candidate, primary, alternate, composite, foreign, surrogate and unique keys, with examples
  • Explain referential integrity and what happens on delete/update of a parent row
  • Normalise a flat table into 1NF, 2NF and 3NF, and know when to denormalise

Why design matters

A database that is designed badly is slow, wastes space and, worst of all, lets data contradict itself. Imagine the customer's city stored in every order row: if the customer moves, you must update thousands of rows, and missing one creates two different "truths". Good design stores each fact once and connects tables with keys.

Entity–Relationship (ER) diagrams

An ER diagram is a picture of the data model before any table is created.

DefinitionBuilding blocks

Entity: a real-world thing you store data about: Customer, Order, Product, Employee. Becomes a table. Attribute: a property of an entity: name, city, price. Becomes a column. Relationship: how entities are associated: a Customer places Orders. Implemented with foreign keys. Cardinality: how many of one entity relate to another: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many. Participation (optionality): whether the relationship is mandatory (every order must have a customer) or optional (a customer may have zero orders).

Crow's-foot notation

The most common notation in industry draws symbols at the ends of each relationship line:

Reading example: Customer ||——o< Order means "each order belongs to exactly one customer; each customer places zero or many orders".

Types of relationships

One-to-one (1:1)

Each row in A matches at most one row in B. Example: Employee ↔ Employee_Bank_Details. Often used to split sensitive or rarely used columns into a separate, more protected table. Implemented with a foreign key that is also unique (often the same as the primary key).

One-to-many (1:N) — the most common

One row in A matches many rows in B; each B row matches one A row. Examples: Customer → Orders, Department → Employees, Category → Products. The foreign key goes on the "many" side (orders.customer_id).

Many-to-many (M:N)

Many rows in A match many in B: Students ↔ Courses, Orders ↔ Products, Actors ↔ Movies. Relational tables cannot store this directly, so we add a junction (bridge, associative) table that holds a pair of foreign keys, turning one M:N into two 1:N relationships.

Relationship Example Where the foreign key goes
1 : 1 Employee – Passport Either side, marked UNIQUE
1 : N Department – Employees On the N side (employees.dept_id)
M : N Students – Courses In a junction table enrolments(student_id, course_id)
Self (recursive) Employee – Manager In the same table: employees.manager_id → employees.emp_id

Let's check the real cardinalities in our retail data with SQL. How many orders does each customer have, and how many items does each order have?

SQL
SELECT MIN(n_orders) AS min_orders_per_customer,
       MAX(n_orders) AS max_orders_per_customer,
       ROUND(AVG(n_orders * 1.0), 2) AS avg_orders_per_customer
FROM (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n_orders FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) AS t;
Result
min_orders_per_customer max_orders_per_customer avg_orders_per_customer
1 10 4.08
1 rows × 3 columns
SQL
SELECT items_in_order, COUNT(*) AS number_of_orders
FROM (SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS items_in_order FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) AS t
GROUP BY items_in_order
ORDER BY items_in_order;
Result
items_in_order number_of_orders
1 1394
2 920
3 455
4 431
4 rows × 2 columns

So Customer → Orders is 1:N, and Order → Order items is 1:N (1 to 4 items per order here).

Keys

Keys are columns (or sets of columns) with special meaning. They are among the most frequently asked interview topics.

Example table employees(emp_id, email, pan_number, name, dept_id, phone), where emp_id, email and pan_number are each unique:

Key type Definition Example
Super key Any set of columns that uniquely identifies a row (may include extra columns) {emp_id}, {emp_id, name}, {email, dept_id}
Candidate key A minimal super key: remove any column and it stops being unique {emp_id}, {email}, {pan_number}
Primary key (PK) The candidate key chosen to identify rows. Unique, not NULL, one per table emp_id
Alternate key Candidate keys not chosen as primary; enforce them with UNIQUE email, pan_number
Composite key A key made of two or more columns (order_id, product_id) in order_items; (student_id, course_id) in enrolments
Foreign key (FK) A column that refers to a PK (or unique key) in another table employees.dept_id → departments.dept_id
Unique key A UNIQUE constraint: no duplicates, but (in SQL Server) one NULL is allowed phone
Surrogate key An artificial key with no business meaning, often an auto-number customer_key INT IDENTITY(1,1)
Natural key A key with business meaning PAN number, GSTIN, ISBN, email
TipSurrogate or natural?

Natural keys can change (people change email, products get recoded) and can be long. Most warehouses and Power BI models use surrogate integer keys for joins, and keep natural keys as alternate (unique) keys.

Primary key vs unique key

Primary key Unique key
Duplicates allowed No No
NULL allowed No Yes (SQL Server allows one NULL; PostgreSQL allows many)
Per table Exactly one Many
Default index (SQL Server) Clustered Non-clustered

Referential integrity

A foreign key guarantees that every child row points to a parent that exists: you cannot insert an order for customer C9999 if that customer does not exist. What happens when a parent row is deleted or its key is updated is controlled by the FK's actions:

Action On DELETE of the parent Use when
NO ACTION (default) The delete is blocked if children exist Most business data
CASCADE Children are deleted too Order → order items
SET NULL Children's FK becomes NULL Employee → manager who leaves
SET DEFAULT Children get the column's default Rare
SQL
CREATE TABLE departments (
    dept_id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    dept_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
CREATE TABLE employees (
    emp_id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
    email      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,          -- alternate key
    name       VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    dept_id    INT NOT NULL REFERENCES departments(dept_id),   -- foreign key
    manager_id INT NULL REFERENCES employees(emp_id)           -- self-referencing FK
);

Lesson 4 shows these constraints in action.

Normalisation

Normalisation organises columns and tables to reduce redundancy and avoid anomalies:

  • Update anomaly: the same fact stored in many rows gets changed in some but not others.
  • Insert anomaly: you cannot add a fact without another fact (cannot add a new product until someone orders it).
  • Delete anomaly: deleting one fact removes another (deleting the only order of a product deletes the product's information).

Start with the flat Superstore file, which repeats customer and product details on every order line:

SQL
SELECT TOP 5 order_id, order_date, customer_id, customer_name, city, product_id, product_name, category, quantity, sales
FROM superstore;
Result
order_id order_date customer_id customer_name city product_id product_name category quantity sales
IN-2023-00001 2023-01-01 C0765 Ishaan Gupta Bengaluru P0059 Nova Phone 223 Technology 2 36,000
IN-2023-00001 2023-01-01 C0765 Ishaan Gupta Bengaluru P0050 Orbit Appliance 798 Office Supplies 1 3,850
IN-2023-00001 2023-01-01 C0765 Ishaan Gupta Bengaluru P0011 Orbit Table 248 Furniture 4 62,080
IN-2023-00002 2023-01-03 C0791 Kabir Singh Ahmedabad P0037 Crest Storage 946 Office Supplies 2 5,216
IN-2023-00003 2023-01-03 C0049 Sneha Khan Ahmedabad P0018 Crest Bookcase 170 Furniture 3 24,591
5 rows × 10 columns

First normal form (1NF)

  • Each cell holds one atomic value (no lists like "Chair, Table").
  • No repeating groups of columns (product1, product2, product3).
  • Each row is unique (a key exists).

The flat file is already in 1NF: one product per row, and every row has a unique row_id. The natural key would be (order_id, product_id), but 70 lines repeat the same product within the same order, which is exactly why real systems add a surrogate key such as row_id or item_id.

Second normal form (2NF)

1NF and every non-key column depends on the whole key, not part of it (this matters only with composite keys). With key (order_id, product_id):

  • quantity, discount, sales depend on both: they stay.
  • order_date, customer_id, ship_mode depend only on order_id → move to an orders table.
  • product_name, category depend only on product_id → move to a products table.

Third normal form (3NF)

2NF and no transitive dependency: non-key columns must depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns. In orders, customer_name, city and region depend on customer_id, not on order_id → move them to a customers table.

"Every non-key attribute must provide a fact about the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key." (Bill Kent)

How much repetition did normalisation remove? Count the distinct customers and products versus rows:

SQL
SELECT COUNT(*)                     AS order_lines,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)     AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)  AS customers,
       COUNT(DISTINCT product_id)   AS products
FROM superstore;
Result
order_lines orders customers products
6323 3200 785 78
1 rows × 4 columns

The flat file stores customer details 6,323 times; the normalised design stores them once per customer (fewer than 800 rows).

Normal form Rule in plain words
1NF One value per cell; no repeating columns; a key exists
2NF No column depends on only part of a composite key
3NF No column depends on another non-key column
BCNF Every determinant is a candidate key (stricter 3NF)
4NF / 5NF Remove multi-valued and join dependencies (rare in practice)

Denormalisation and the star schema

Transactional systems (OLTP) are normalised for safe, fast writes. Analytical systems (OLAP, data warehouses, Power BI) are often denormalised into a star schema: one central fact table (sales events with numbers) surrounded by dimension tables (customer, product, date, region) to make reading and aggregating fast and simple. You will build one in the Power BI track (Lesson 3).

OLTP (normalised) OLAP / warehouse (star schema)
Purpose Run the business: place orders, update stock Analyse the business
Operations Many small inserts and updates Large reads and aggregations
Design 3NF, many tables Fact + dimension tables
Examples App database in SQL Server/PostgreSQL Snowflake, BigQuery, Fabric, Power BI model

Summary

Key takeaways
  • ER diagrams show entities (tables), attributes (columns) and relationships with cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N).
  • The foreign key sits on the many side; M:N needs a junction table with a composite key.
  • Super key ⊇ candidate keys (minimal); one candidate becomes the primary key (unique, not NULL), the others are alternate keys (UNIQUE).
  • Composite keys combine columns; surrogate keys are artificial integers; natural keys carry business meaning.
  • Foreign keys enforce referential integrity; ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL / NO ACTION decide what happens to children.
  • Normalise to 3NF to remove redundancy and anomalies; denormalise into a star schema for analytics.
Quick quiz6 questions · tap an answer to check it

1. Students can enrol in many courses and courses have many students. How do you model this?

Answer: C. A junction table resolves M:N into two 1:N relationships.

2. In a 1:N relationship between departments and employees, where does the foreign key go?

Answer: B. The FK goes on the "many" side: employees.dept_id.

3. Which statement about a primary key is FALSE?

Answer: C. A table has one primary key, which may be composite.

4. email is unique in the employees table but emp_id was chosen as the primary key. What is email?

Answer: B. Unchosen candidate keys are alternate keys, enforced with UNIQUE.

5. In orders(order_id, customer_id, customer_city), customer_city depends on customer_id. Which normal form is violated?

Answer: C. A non-key column depending on another non-key column is a transitive dependency, violating 3NF.

6. What does ON DELETE CASCADE on order_items.order_id do?

Answer: A. CASCADE propagates the delete to child rows.
ExerciseDesign a library database

A library has members, books and loans. A member can borrow many books over time; a book (copy) can be borrowed many times; each loan has a borrow date, due date and return date. Books have an ISBN, title and author; authors can write many books and a book can have several authors. Draw the entities, keys and relationships.

Show solution
  • members(member_id PK, name, email UNIQUE, phone)
  • books(book_id PK, isbn UNIQUE, title, publisher, year)
  • authors(author_id PK, name)
  • book_authors(book_id FK, author_id FK, PRIMARY KEY (book_id, author_id)): junction for M:N.
  • copies(copy_id PK, book_id FK, shelf): one book has many physical copies.
  • loans(loan_id PK, copy_id FK, member_id FK, borrow_date, due_date, return_date NULL). Relationships: members 1:N loans; copies 1:N loans; books 1:N copies; books M:N authors (via book_authors).
Interview cornerQuestions you may be asked

Q: Difference between primary key, unique key and foreign key? PK uniquely identifies rows, no NULLs, one per table. A unique key also prevents duplicates but allows a NULL (one in SQL Server) and a table can have many. A foreign key references a PK/unique key in another table to enforce relationships.

Q: What is a candidate key? A composite key? A candidate key is a minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies rows; one is chosen as the PK. A composite key uses two or more columns together, such as (order_id, product_id).

Q: What is normalisation and why denormalise? Normalisation removes redundancy and anomalies (1NF–3NF). Data warehouses denormalise into star schemas to make analytical queries simpler and faster.

SQL for Data Analysis · Lesson 3

Data Types, Operators, NULLs, Variables & Comments

Choose the right SQL Server data type for every column, use arithmetic, comparison, logical and string operators correctly, understand NULL and three-valued logic, declare variables, follow naming rules and write readable, commented SQL.

● SQL class 2✦ SQL Server 2022, 2026Beginner⏱ 100 min
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Pick suitable numeric, text, date/time and other data types, and know why the choice matters
  • Use arithmetic, comparison, logical and concatenation operators, including integer division and modulo
  • Explain NULL, three-valued logic, IS NULL and COALESCE
  • Declare and use T-SQL variables with DECLARE, SET and SELECT
  • Follow identifier naming rules and conventions, and comment code

Why data types matter

Every column has exactly one data type. The type decides what values are allowed, how much storage they use, how they sort and compare, and which functions work on them. A column of dates stored as text sorts "01-02-2026" before "31-01-2025" and cannot be used for date arithmetic, the same problem you met in Excel.

SQL Server data types

Numbers

Type Range / precision Storage Use for
TINYINT 0 to 255 1 byte Ratings, small codes
SMALLINT −32,768 to 32,767 2 bytes Small counts
INT about ±2.1 billion 4 bytes IDs, quantities (default choice)
BIGINT about ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ 8 bytes Very large IDs, event logs
DECIMAL(p, s) / NUMERIC exact, p digits with s after the point 5–17 bytes Money, rates: DECIMAL(12,2) holds up to 9,999,999,999.99
MONEY exact, 4 decimals 8 bytes Currency (DECIMAL is more portable)
FLOAT, REAL approximate binary floating point 8 / 4 bytes Scientific measurements, ML scores
BIT 0, 1 or NULL 1 bit Yes/No flags
Watch outNever store money in FLOAT

FLOAT cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly (0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3), so totals drift by tiny amounts. Use DECIMAL(p, s) for currency.

Text

Type Description Example
CHAR(n) Fixed length, padded with spaces CHAR(2) for state codes MH
VARCHAR(n) Variable length, up to n bytes (n ≤ 8000) VARCHAR(100) for names in English
NVARCHAR(n) Variable length Unicode (Hindi, Tamil, emoji) NVARCHAR(100) for names in any language
VARCHAR(MAX), NVARCHAR(MAX) Up to 2 GB Long descriptions, JSON

Prefix Unicode string literals with N: N'नमस्ते'. Without N, non-Latin characters can turn into ?.

Dates and times

Type Stores Example
DATE Date only 2026-04-27
TIME Time only 14:30:00
DATETIME2(p) Date + time, precise (preferred) 2026-04-27 14:30:15.1234567
DATETIME Older date + time (3.33 ms precision) Legacy tables
DATETIMEOFFSET Date + time + time zone 2026-04-27 14:30 +05:30
SMALLDATETIME Date + time to the minute Low-precision logs

Always write date literals in the unambiguous ISO format 'YYYY-MM-DD' ('2026-04-27'). '04/05/2026' means April 5 or May 4 depending on the server's language settings.

Others

UNIQUEIDENTIFIER (GUIDs), VARBINARY (files, images), XML, JSON stored in NVARCHAR(MAX) with JSON functions, GEOGRAPHY (maps), and from SQL Server 2025 a native VECTOR type for AI embeddings.

Choosing types for the retail tables

Column Good type Why
customer_id VARCHAR(10) Codes like C0001 keep leading letters/zeros
customer_name NVARCHAR(100) Names in any language
order_date DATE No time needed
quantity INT (or SMALLINT) Whole numbers
discount DECIMAL(4,2) 0.00 to 0.99 exactly
sales, profit DECIMAL(12,2) Money
is_returned BIT Yes/No

Here are the types DuckDB inferred when loading the CSV (SSMS's Import Flat File wizard does the same kind of guessing; always review its suggestions):

Output
column_name column_type
0 row_id BIGINT
1 order_id VARCHAR
2 order_date DATE
3 ship_date DATE
4 ship_mode VARCHAR
5 customer_id VARCHAR
6 customer_name VARCHAR
7 segment VARCHAR
8 city VARCHAR
9 state VARCHAR
10 region VARCHAR
11 product_id VARCHAR
19 rows × 2 columns (first 12 shown)

Operators

Arithmetic

Operator Meaning Example Result in SQL Server
+ Add SELECT 7 + 2 9
- Subtract SELECT 7 - 2 5
* Multiply SELECT 7 * 2 14
/ Divide SELECT 7 / 2 3 (integer ÷ integer = integer)
/ Divide SELECT 7 / 2.0 3.500000
% Modulo (remainder) SELECT 7 % 2 1
Common mistakesInteger division

In SQL Server, dividing two integers drops the decimals: SELECT 1/3 returns 0, and COUNT(...)/COUNT(...) returns 0 or 1 instead of a percentage. Multiply by 1.0 or CAST one side: SELECT 100.0 * returned / total or CAST(returned AS DECIMAL(10,2)) / total. (PostgreSQL behaves the same way; MySQL and DuckDB return decimals.)

Calculated columns are written right in the SELECT list. Here is unit price and margin for a few order lines:

SQL
SELECT TOP 6
       order_id,
       quantity,
       sales,
       profit,
       ROUND(sales / quantity, 2)          AS unit_price,
       ROUND(100.0 * profit / sales, 1)    AS margin_pct
FROM superstore
ORDER BY row_id;
Result
order_id quantity sales profit unit_price margin_pct
IN-2023-00001 2 36,000 3,472.55 18,000 9.6
IN-2023-00001 1 3,850 1,169.54 3,850 30.4
IN-2023-00001 4 62,080 6,044.47 15,520 9.7
IN-2023-00002 2 5,216 450.16 2,608 8.6
IN-2023-00003 3 24,591 -5,512.33 8,197 -22.4
IN-2023-00003 1 8,288 -1,598.43 8,288 -19.3
6 rows × 6 columns

Comparison

Operator Meaning
= Equal
<> or != Not equal
> < >= <= Greater / less (than or equal)
BETWEEN a AND b Inclusive range
IN (…) Matches any value in a list
LIKE Pattern match with % and _
IS NULL / IS NOT NULL Tests for missing values

Logical

AND (both true), OR (at least one true), NOT (reverses). Precedence: NOT first, then AND, then OR. Use brackets to make intent obvious.

SQL
-- Without brackets, AND is evaluated first:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_without_brackets
FROM superstore
WHERE region = 'North' OR region = 'South' AND category = 'Technology';
Result
rows_without_brackets
2025
1 rows × 1 columns
SQL
-- With brackets: (North or South) and Technology
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_with_brackets
FROM superstore
WHERE (region = 'North' OR region = 'South') AND category = 'Technology';
Result
rows_with_brackets
952
1 rows × 1 columns

The first query returns all North rows plus South Technology rows: probably not what was meant. Brackets fix it.

String concatenation

Method Example NULL behaviour
+ first_name + ' ' + last_name Any NULL makes the whole result NULL
CONCAT() CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) Treats NULL as empty text
CONCAT_WS() CONCAT_WS(', ', city, state, 'India') Separator; skips NULLs
SQL
SELECT TOP 4 customer_name,
       CONCAT(city, ', ', state)            AS city_state,
       CONCAT_WS(' | ', segment, region)    AS segment_region
FROM customers;
Result
customer_name city_state segment_region
Saanvi Khan Chandigarh, Punjab Corporate | North
Meera Bose Delhi, Delhi Corporate | North
Riya Shah Kolkata, West Bengal Consumer | East
Diya Fernandes Indore, Madhya Pradesh Corporate | West
4 rows × 3 columns

NULL: the missing value

NULL means unknown or missing. It is not zero and not an empty string. Any comparison with NULL returns UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE. SQL uses three-valued logic:

Expression Result
NULL = NULL UNKNOWN
NULL <> 5 UNKNOWN
5 + NULL NULL
TRUE AND UNKNOWN UNKNOWN
FALSE AND UNKNOWN FALSE
TRUE OR UNKNOWN TRUE
NOT UNKNOWN UNKNOWN

WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE, so rows where it is UNKNOWN disappear silently. That is why you must test with IS NULL:

SQL
WITH t AS (
    SELECT 'A' AS item, 10 AS score UNION ALL
    SELECT 'B', NULL UNION ALL
    SELECT 'C', 30
)
SELECT
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE score = NULL)   AS equals_null_rows,     -- always 0!
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE score IS NULL)  AS is_null_rows,
    (SELECT COUNT(score) FROM t)                  AS count_score,          -- ignores NULL
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t)                      AS count_star,
    (SELECT AVG(score * 1.0) FROM t)              AS avg_ignores_null,     -- (10+30)/2
    (SELECT AVG(COALESCE(score, 0) * 1.0) FROM t) AS avg_null_as_zero;     -- (10+0+30)/3
Result
equals_null_rows is_null_rows count_score count_star avg_ignores_null avg_null_as_zero
0 1 2 3 20 13.33
1 rows × 6 columns
Function What it does
ISNULL(x, y) T-SQL: return y when x is NULL
COALESCE(x, y, z, …) ANSI: the first non-NULL value; works in every database
NULLIF(a, b) NULL if a = b, otherwise a. Classic use: sales / NULLIF(qty, 0) avoids divide-by-zero errors

Variables in T-SQL

T-SQL lets you store a value in a variable for the length of a batch. Variable names start with @.

SQL
DECLARE @target_region VARCHAR(20) = 'West';     -- declare and assign
DECLARE @min_sales     DECIMAL(12,2);
SET @min_sales = 50000;                           -- assign with SET

SELECT order_id, city, sales
FROM superstore
WHERE region = @target_region AND sales >= @min_sales;

DECLARE @total DECIMAL(14,2);
SELECT @total = SUM(sales) FROM superstore;       -- assign from a query
PRINT CONCAT('Total sales: ', @total);            -- message in the Messages tab

Variables make scripts reusable (change 'West' once) and are the basis of stored procedures (Lesson 13). Other databases use different syntax (PostgreSQL DO blocks or \set in psql).

Identifiers: naming rules and conventions

Rules (SQL Server): - Start with a letter, _, @ (variables) or # (temporary tables). - Up to 128 characters; letters, digits, _, @, $, #. - Reserved words (ORDER, GROUP, USER) and names with spaces must be wrapped in [square brackets] (or "double quotes"): [Order Details], [order].

Conventions used in this handbook (pick one style and be consistent): - snake_case, lowercase table and column names: order_items, customer_id. - Plural table names (customers) or singular (customer): be consistent. - Primary key id or <table>_id; foreign keys named after the referenced key (customer_id). - Prefix views vw_, procedures usp_, indexes ix_. - Avoid spaces, special characters and reserved words, so you never need brackets.

Comments and formatting

SQL
-- A single-line comment: everything after -- is ignored

/* A multi-line comment:
   Purpose : Top 10 customers by 2025 sales
   Author  : Varun Kumar
   Updated : 27-Apr-2026                         */

SELECT TOP 10
       customer_id,
       SUM(sales) AS total_sales           -- revenue in rupees
FROM   superstore
WHERE  order_date >= '2025-01-01'
  AND  order_date <  '2026-01-01'          -- half-open range: safe with times
GROUP  BY customer_id
ORDER  BY total_sales DESC;
TipReadable SQL checklist

One clause per line (SELECT, FROM, WHERE…), one column per line in long queries, consistent indentation, keywords in capitals, meaningful aliases, and a header comment explaining the purpose. Tools such as the "Format SQL" extension or SQLFluff format code automatically.

Summary

Key takeaways
  • Choose types deliberately: INT for IDs and counts, DECIMAL(p,s) for money, NVARCHAR for names, DATE/DATETIME2 for dates; never FLOAT for money.
  • Write dates as 'YYYY-MM-DD'.
  • 7/2 = 3 in SQL Server: use 1.0 * or CAST for decimal division; % gives the remainder.
  • Precedence: NOT, AND, OR; use brackets.
  • NULL is unknown: compare with IS NULL; aggregates ignore NULLs; COALESCE, ISNULL and NULLIF handle them.
  • CONCAT treats NULL as empty; + with a NULL returns NULL.
  • Variables: DECLARE @x type = value; name things consistently and comment your code.
Quick quiz6 questions · tap an answer to check it

1. Which data type should store a product price in rupees and paise?

Answer: C. DECIMAL stores exact decimal values, which money needs.

2. In SQL Server, what does SELECT 9 / 4 return?

Answer: A. Integer divided by integer gives an integer (the fraction is dropped).

3. What does WHERE discount = NULL return?

Answer: B. Comparisons with NULL are UNKNOWN, so WHERE keeps nothing. Use IS NULL.

4. Which expression returns 'Pune' when city is NULL?

Answer: B. COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value.

5. WHERE a = 1 OR b = 2 AND c = 3 is evaluated as:

Answer: B. AND has higher precedence than OR.

6. Why use NVARCHAR instead of VARCHAR for customer names?

Answer: B. NVARCHAR stores Unicode text; VARCHAR may lose characters outside the code page.
ExerciseFix the query

A colleague wrote: SELECT order_id, profit/sales*100 AS margin FROM superstore WHERE category = 'Furniture' OR category = 'Technology' AND discount > 0.2 AND ship_mode = NULL; List every problem and rewrite it.

Show solution
  1. AND binds before OR, so the discount and ship-mode filters apply only to Technology: add brackets.
  2. ship_mode = NULL never matches: use IS NULL (or remove it if not needed).
  3. If profit and sales were integers, profit/sales would be integer division; use 100.0 * profit / sales and guard against zero with NULLIF(sales, 0). Rewritten: SELECT order_id, ROUND(100.0 * profit / NULLIF(sales, 0), 1) AS margin_pct FROM superstore WHERE category IN ('Furniture', 'Technology') AND discount > 0.2;
Interview cornerQuestions you may be asked

Q: What is the difference between CHAR, VARCHAR and NVARCHAR? CHAR is fixed length (padded), VARCHAR is variable length non-Unicode, NVARCHAR is variable length Unicode (two bytes per character for most scripts).

Q: How does SQL treat NULL? As unknown: comparisons return UNKNOWN, aggregates (except COUNT(*)) ignore NULLs, arithmetic with NULL returns NULL. Use IS NULL, COALESCE/ISNULL and NULLIF.

Q: Why does SELECT 100 * returned / total give 0? Integer division when both values are integers; cast to decimal or multiply by 100.0.

Q: DECIMAL vs FLOAT? DECIMAL is exact (money, rates); FLOAT is approximate binary (scientific values) and can introduce rounding errors.

SQL for Data Analysis · Lesson 4

DDL, DML & Constraints: CREATE, ALTER, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

Create and change tables with DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE), add, change and remove rows with DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE), protect data quality with constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT, IDENTITY) and understand DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP.

● SQL classes 2–3✦ SQL Server 2022, 2026Beginner⏱ 120 min
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Create databases and tables with appropriate data types and constraints
  • Modify table structure with ALTER TABLE (add, change, drop columns and constraints)
  • Insert single and multiple rows, insert from a query, update and delete rows safely
  • Explain every constraint type and read the error each one raises
  • Compare DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP, and use MERGE for upserts

The life cycle of a table

CREATE TABLE

SQL
CREATE TABLE departments (
    dept_id    INT          PRIMARY KEY,
    dept_name  VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    location   VARCHAR(50)  DEFAULT 'Bengaluru'
);

CREATE TABLE staff (
    emp_id     INT            PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name  VARCHAR(100)   NOT NULL,
    email      VARCHAR(100)   NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    dept_id    INT            NOT NULL REFERENCES departments(dept_id),
    salary     DECIMAL(10,2)  CHECK (salary > 0),
    join_date  DATE           DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE,
    is_active  BOOLEAN        DEFAULT TRUE
);
Result
Commands completed successfully.
Commands completed successfully.

In SQL Server you would usually write IDENTITY(1,1) for an auto-numbered key, BIT for the flag and DEFAULT GETDATE() for today. Here is the same staff table in full T-SQL style, with named constraints (names make error messages and later changes much easier):

SQL
CREATE TABLE dbo.staff (
    emp_id     INT IDENTITY(1,1)  NOT NULL,
    full_name  NVARCHAR(100)      NOT NULL,
    email      VARCHAR(100)       NOT NULL,
    dept_id    INT                NOT NULL,
    salary     DECIMAL(10,2)      NULL,
    join_date  DATE               NOT NULL CONSTRAINT df_staff_join  DEFAULT (CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)),
    is_active  BIT                NOT NULL CONSTRAINT df_staff_active DEFAULT (1),
    CONSTRAINT pk_staff         PRIMARY KEY (emp_id),
    CONSTRAINT uq_staff_email   UNIQUE (email),
    CONSTRAINT fk_staff_dept    FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES dbo.departments(dept_id),
    CONSTRAINT ck_staff_salary  CHECK (salary > 0)
);

Constraints at a glance

Constraint Guarantees Example
PRIMARY KEY Unique and not NULL; identifies each row emp_id
FOREIGN KEY / REFERENCES Value must exist in the parent table dept_id → departments
UNIQUE No duplicate values (NULL allowed once in SQL Server) email
NOT NULL A value is required full_name
CHECK Value must satisfy a condition salary > 0, discount BETWEEN 0 AND 0.9
DEFAULT Value used when none is supplied is_active = 1
IDENTITY(seed, step) Auto-numbering (SQL Server) IDENTITY(1,1)

INSERT: adding rows

SQL
INSERT INTO departments (dept_id, dept_name, location) VALUES
    (10, 'Finance', 'Mumbai'),
    (20, 'IT',      'Pune'),
    (30, 'HR',      DEFAULT),
    (40, 'Sales',   'Delhi');

INSERT INTO staff (emp_id, full_name, email, dept_id, salary, join_date) VALUES
    (1, 'Kavya Iyer',        'kavya@abc.in',    30,  97000, '2016-02-28'),
    (2, 'Imran Reddy',       'imran@abc.in',    10, 157000, '2019-12-14'),
    (3, 'Harpreet Kulkarni', 'harpreet@abc.in', 10, 131000, '2024-10-05'),
    (4, 'Rahul Iyer',        'rahul@abc.in',    20, 112000, '2017-02-06'),
    (5, 'Isha Mehta',        'isha@abc.in',     40,  57000, '2021-09-07');

SELECT * FROM departments;
Result
(4 rows affected)
(5 rows affected)
dept_id dept_name location
10 Finance Mumbai
20 IT Pune
30 HR Bengaluru
40 Sales Delhi
4 rows × 3 columns
SQL
SELECT emp_id, full_name, dept_id, salary, join_date, is_active FROM staff;
Result
emp_id full_name dept_id salary join_date is_active
1 Kavya Iyer 30 97,000 2016-02-28 True
2 Imran Reddy 10 157,000 2019-12-14 True
3 Harpreet Kulkarni 10 131,000 2024-10-05 True
4 Rahul Iyer 20 112,000 2017-02-06 True
5 Isha Mehta 40 57,000 2021-09-07 True
5 rows × 6 columns

DEFAULT filled HR's location with Bengaluru and every employee's is_active with TRUE.

TipAlways list the columns

INSERT INTO staff VALUES (…) without a column list depends on the column order and breaks the day someone adds a column. Always write INSERT INTO staff (col1, col2, …) VALUES (…).

INSERT … SELECT and SELECT … INTO

Copy rows from a query into a table:

SQL
-- Into an existing table
INSERT INTO staff_archive (emp_id, full_name, dept_id, salary)
SELECT emp_id, full_name, dept_id, salary
FROM staff
WHERE is_active = 0;

-- SQL Server: create a NEW table from a query (structure + data, no constraints)
SELECT emp_id, full_name, salary
INTO   staff_backup_2026
FROM   staff;

The portable equivalent of SELECT … INTO is CREATE TABLE new_table AS SELECT … (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Snowflake, DuckDB).

What constraints do when rules are broken

Constraints reject bad data at the database, whatever app or person sends it. These statements would all fail in SQL Server with the messages shown (abridged):

Statement Broken rule SQL Server message
INSERT INTO departments VALUES (10,'Ops','Pune') PRIMARY KEY Violation of PRIMARY KEY constraint 'pk_departments'. Cannot insert duplicate key … The duplicate key value is (10).
INSERT INTO staff (…, email, …) VALUES (…, 'kavya@abc.in', …) UNIQUE Violation of UNIQUE KEY constraint 'uq_staff_email'. Cannot insert duplicate key …
INSERT INTO staff (…, dept_id, …) VALUES (…, 99, …) FOREIGN KEY The INSERT statement conflicted with the FOREIGN KEY constraint "fk_staff_dept".
INSERT INTO staff (emp_id, email, dept_id) VALUES (9,'x@abc.in',10) NOT NULL Cannot insert the value NULL into column 'full_name' … column does not allow nulls. INSERT fails.
UPDATE staff SET salary = -500 WHERE emp_id = 1 CHECK The UPDATE statement conflicted with the CHECK constraint "ck_staff_salary".
DELETE FROM departments WHERE dept_id = 10 FOREIGN KEY (children exist) The DELETE statement conflicted with the REFERENCE constraint "fk_staff_dept".

Our practice engine raises the same kind of error. For example, trying to add an employee to a department that does not exist:

Output
Error: Constraint Error: Violates foreign key constraint because key "dept_id: 99" does not exist in the referenced table

UPDATE: changing rows

SQL
-- Give everyone in Finance a 5% raise
UPDATE staff
SET    salary = salary * 1.05
WHERE  dept_id = 10;

-- Change two columns for one person
UPDATE staff
SET    dept_id = 20, salary = 60000
WHERE  emp_id = 5;

SELECT emp_id, full_name, dept_id, salary FROM staff ORDER BY emp_id;
Result
(2 rows affected)
(1 row affected)
emp_id full_name dept_id salary
1 Kavya Iyer 30 97,000
2 Imran Reddy 10 164,850
3 Harpreet Kulkarni 10 137,550
4 Rahul Iyer 20 112,000
5 Isha Mehta 20 60,000
5 rows × 4 columns
Watch outUPDATE or DELETE without WHERE changes EVERY row

UPDATE staff SET salary = 0; sets every salary to zero. Before any UPDATE or DELETE: 1. Write the WHERE first and run it as a SELECT to see exactly which rows will change. 2. Wrap the change in a transaction (BEGIN TRAN … then check, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK) (Lesson 14). 3. On production data, take a backup or work in a copy.

UPDATE with a join (SQL Server)

SQL
-- Mark staff in Mumbai departments as 'on-site'
UPDATE s
SET    s.work_mode = 'on-site'
FROM   staff AS s
JOIN   departments AS d ON d.dept_id = s.dept_id
WHERE  d.location = 'Mumbai';

DELETE: removing rows

SQL
DELETE FROM staff
WHERE emp_id = 5;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS staff_left FROM staff;
Result
(1 row affected)
staff_left
4
1 rows × 1 columns

ALTER TABLE: changing structure

SQL
ALTER TABLE staff ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(15);
ALTER TABLE staff ADD COLUMN work_mode VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'hybrid';
SELECT emp_id, full_name, phone, work_mode FROM staff;
Result
emp_id full_name phone work_mode
1 Kavya Iyer NULL hybrid
2 Imran Reddy NULL hybrid
3 Harpreet Kulkarni NULL hybrid
4 Rahul Iyer NULL hybrid
4 rows × 4 columns

The SQL Server forms of the common changes:

SQL
ALTER TABLE staff ADD phone VARCHAR(15) NULL;                        -- add a column (no COLUMN keyword in T-SQL)
ALTER TABLE staff ALTER COLUMN full_name NVARCHAR(150) NOT NULL;     -- change type / nullability
ALTER TABLE staff DROP COLUMN phone;                                 -- remove a column
ALTER TABLE staff ADD CONSTRAINT ck_staff_mode CHECK (work_mode IN ('remote','hybrid','on-site'));
ALTER TABLE staff DROP CONSTRAINT ck_staff_mode;                     -- remove a constraint by name
EXEC sp_rename 'staff.full_name', 'employee_name', 'COLUMN';         -- rename a column
EXEC sp_rename 'staff', 'employees_master';                          -- rename a table
NoteChanging a column that has data

Making a column smaller (VARCHAR(100) → VARCHAR(10)) fails if existing values do not fit; adding NOT NULL fails if NULLs exist. Clean the data first, or add a DEFAULT.

DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP

This is one of the most common SQL interview questions.

DELETE TRUNCATE TABLE DROP TABLE
Family DML DDL DDL
Removes Some or all rows All rows The whole table: rows, structure, indexes, constraints, permissions
WHERE allowed Yes No No
Speed on large tables Slower: logs each row Very fast: deallocates pages Fast
Logging Every row logged Minimal (page deallocations) Minimal
Fires DELETE triggers Yes No No
Resets IDENTITY No Yes, back to the seed Table is gone
Works when referenced by a FK Yes (if no child rows violate it) No No (drop the FK first)
Can be rolled back in a transaction Yes Yes in SQL Server (inside an explicit transaction) Yes in SQL Server (inside an explicit transaction)
SQL
CREATE TABLE temp_log (id INT, msg VARCHAR(50));
INSERT INTO temp_log VALUES (1, 'start'), (2, 'load'), (3, 'end');
DELETE FROM temp_log WHERE id = 2;           -- removes one row
SELECT COUNT(*) AS after_delete FROM temp_log;
Result
Commands completed successfully.
(3 rows affected)
(1 row affected)
after_delete
2
1 rows × 1 columns
SQL
TRUNCATE TABLE temp_log;                      -- removes all rows, keeps the table
SELECT COUNT(*) AS after_truncate FROM temp_log;
Result
after_truncate
0
1 rows × 1 columns
SQL
DROP TABLE temp_log;                          -- removes the table itself
SELECT COUNT(*) AS tables_named_temp_log FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name = 'temp_log';
Result
tables_named_temp_log
0
1 rows × 1 columns

In SQL Server, DROP TABLE IF EXISTS temp_log; avoids an error when the table is already gone.

MERGE: insert or update in one statement (upsert)

Data pipelines often receive a file of changes: some rows are new, others update existing rows. MERGE handles both:

SQL
MERGE dbo.staff AS target
USING dbo.staff_updates AS src
      ON target.emp_id = src.emp_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN
     UPDATE SET target.salary = src.salary, target.dept_id = src.dept_id
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
     INSERT (emp_id, full_name, email, dept_id, salary)
     VALUES (src.emp_id, src.full_name, src.email, src.dept_id, src.salary)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN
     UPDATE SET target.is_active = 0;          -- in staff but not in the file

Loading CSV files with SQL

SQL
CREATE TABLE dbo.employees_small (
    emp_id VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, name NVARCHAR(100), department VARCHAR(30),
    city VARCHAR(30), join_date DATE, salary DECIMAL(10,2), rating TINYINT
);

BULK INSERT dbo.employees_small
FROM 'C:\Data\employees_small.csv'
WITH (FORMAT = 'CSV', FIRSTROW = 2, FIELDTERMINATOR = ',', ROWTERMINATOR = '0x0a');

The SSMS Import Flat File wizard is easier for one-off loads; BULK INSERT, bcp or an ETL tool (SSIS, Azure Data Factory, Fabric pipelines) are used for repeatable loads.

Do it with AIDo it with AI

Ask: "Write SQL Server CREATE TABLE statements with constraints for a hospital database: patients, doctors, appointments (a patient can see many doctors; a doctor sees many patients). Include primary keys, foreign keys, CHECK constraints for appointment status, and sensible data types." Then review it: are the keys right, is money DECIMAL, are dates DATE/DATETIME2, are the constraints named?

Summary

Key takeaways
  • DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE change structure. DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE change rows.
  • Constraints (PK, FK, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT, IDENTITY) protect data quality at the source; name them.
  • Always list columns in INSERT; always test the WHERE of an UPDATE/DELETE with a SELECT first, inside a transaction.
  • DELETE removes chosen rows (logged, triggers fire); TRUNCATE empties the table fast and resets IDENTITY; DROP removes the table.
  • MERGE performs upserts; BULK INSERT and the Import wizard load files.
Quick quiz6 questions · tap an answer to check it

1. Which statement removes all rows but keeps the table structure and resets the IDENTITY counter?

Answer: B. TRUNCATE empties the table quickly and resets IDENTITY to its seed.

2. You run UPDATE staff SET salary = 50000; by mistake. What happened?

Answer: B. Without WHERE, UPDATE changes every row. Use transactions and test with SELECT first.

3. Which constraint stops a salary of −500?

Answer: C. CHECK validates values against a condition.

4. Inserting an employee with dept_id 99 fails with a FOREIGN KEY error. Why?

Answer: B. A foreign key value must exist in the referenced table.

5. Which is TRUE about DELETE?

Answer: A. DELETE is DML, works row by row with a WHERE, and fires triggers.

6. How do you add a column phone to staff in SQL Server?

Answer: B. T-SQL uses ADD without the COLUMN keyword (PostgreSQL/MySQL accept ADD COLUMN).
ExerciseBuild and populate a small schema

Create projects(project_id PK, name UNIQUE NOT NULL, budget DECIMAL(12,2) CHECK budget ≥ 0, start_date DATE, status with CHECK IN ('planned','active','closed') DEFAULT 'planned') and assignments(project_id FK, emp_id FK, role, hours, PRIMARY KEY (project_id, emp_id)). Insert 3 projects and 4 assignments, raise the budget of active projects by 10%, close one project, and delete assignments of closed projects.

Show solution
SQL
CREATE TABLE projects (
  project_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  budget DECIMAL(12,2) CHECK (budget >= 0), start_date DATE,
  status VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'planned' CHECK (status IN ('planned','active','closed')));
CREATE TABLE assignments (
  project_id INT REFERENCES projects(project_id), emp_id INT REFERENCES staff(emp_id),
  role VARCHAR(30), hours INT CHECK (hours > 0), PRIMARY KEY (project_id, emp_id));
INSERT INTO projects (project_id, name, budget, start_date, status) VALUES
  (1,'CRM revamp',2500000,'2026-01-10','active'), (2,'Payroll audit',600000,'2026-03-01','active'), (3,'Data lake',4000000,'2026-06-01','planned');
INSERT INTO assignments VALUES (1,1,'Analyst',120),(1,4,'Developer',300),(2,2,'Lead',80),(3,3,'Architect',40);
UPDATE projects SET budget = budget * 1.10 WHERE status = 'active';
UPDATE projects SET status = 'closed' WHERE project_id = 2;
DELETE FROM assignments WHERE project_id IN (SELECT project_id FROM projects WHERE status = 'closed');
Interview cornerQuestions you may be asked

Q: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP? DELETE (DML) removes chosen rows with WHERE, logs each row, fires triggers and keeps IDENTITY. TRUNCATE (DDL) removes all rows quickly, minimal logging, resets IDENTITY, no WHERE, not allowed when referenced by a FK. DROP removes the whole table and its definition.

Q: What are constraints and why use them instead of app validation? Rules enforced by the database (PK, FK, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT). They protect data no matter which app, script or person writes to the table.

Q: How do you safely run an UPDATE on production? Run the WHERE as a SELECT first, wrap in BEGIN TRAN, check @@ROWCOUNT and the result, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK; have a backup.

SQL for Data Analysis · Lesson 5

SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY & Filtering Operators

Retrieve exactly the rows and columns you need. Master SELECT, aliases with AS, DISTINCT, TOP, WHERE with comparison and logical operators, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE wildcards, IS NULL, ORDER BY, and the logical order in which SQL processes a query.

● SQL class 3✦ SQL Server 2022, 2026Beginner⏱ 120 min
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Select columns, calculated expressions and aliases, and remove duplicates with DISTINCT
  • Filter rows with comparison, logical, IN, NOT IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, NOT LIKE, IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
  • Sort results by one or more columns, expressions and positions; limit rows with TOP
  • Explain the logical processing order of a query and why it matters for aliases
  • Translate business questions into correct SELECT statements

The shape of a SELECT statement

SQL
SELECT   column_list            -- what to show
FROM     table_name             -- where it comes from
WHERE    row_conditions         -- which rows to keep
GROUP BY grouping_columns       -- (Lesson 7)
HAVING   group_conditions       -- (Lesson 7)
ORDER BY sort_columns;          -- how to sort the result

Only SELECT is required (SELECT 1 + 1; works). Everything else is optional but must appear in this order.

SELECT: columns, expressions and aliases

SQL
SELECT TOP 5
       order_id,
       order_date,
       customer_name,
       sales,
       profit,
       sales - profit                     AS cost,
       ROUND(100.0 * profit / sales, 1)   AS margin_pct,
       'INR'                              AS currency
FROM superstore;
Result
order_id order_date customer_name sales profit cost margin_pct currency
IN-2023-00001 2023-01-01 Ishaan Gupta 36,000 3,472.55 32,527.45 9.6 INR
IN-2023-00001 2023-01-01 Ishaan Gupta 3,850 1,169.54 2,680.46 30.4 INR
IN-2023-00001 2023-01-01 Ishaan Gupta 62,080 6,044.47 56,035.53 9.7 INR
IN-2023-00002 2023-01-03 Kabir Singh 5,216 450.16 4,765.84 8.6 INR
IN-2023-00003 2023-01-03 Sneha Khan 24,591 -5,512.33 30,103.33 -22.4 INR
5 rows × 8 columns
  • SELECT * returns every column. Use it to explore, never in production code (it breaks when columns change and reads more data than needed).
  • An alias renames a column or table in the result: AS margin_pct. AS is optional (sales - profit cost) but makes code clearer. Aliases with spaces need brackets or quotes: AS [Margin %].
  • Expressions can use operators, functions and literals.

Table aliases

SQL
SELECT s.order_id, s.sales
FROM superstore AS s;          -- 's' is a short name for the table

Table aliases become essential with joins (Lesson 8).

DISTINCT: unique values

SQL
SELECT DISTINCT region
FROM superstore
ORDER BY region;
Result
region
East
North
South
West
4 rows × 1 columns
SQL
SELECT DISTINCT category, sub_category
FROM superstore
ORDER BY category, sub_category;
Result
category sub_category
Furniture Bookcases
Furniture Chairs
Furniture Furnishings
Furniture Tables
Office Supplies Appliances
Office Supplies Art
Office Supplies Binders
Office Supplies Paper
Office Supplies Storage
Technology Accessories
Technology Copiers
Technology Machines
13 rows × 2 columns (first 12 shown)

DISTINCT applies to the whole row of selected columns: the second query returns each category–sub-category combination once. To count unique values: COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id).

TOP: limit the rows

SQL
SELECT TOP 5 order_id, customer_name, city, sales
FROM superstore
ORDER BY sales DESC;
Result
order_id customer_name city sales
IN-2024-01857 Arjun Fernandes Delhi 619,290
IN-2023-00564 Krishna Reddy Hyderabad 551,530
IN-2024-01040 Aditya Kulkarni Chennai 551,530
IN-2025-02880 Farhan Khan Kochi 530,820
IN-2023-00809 Rohan Singh Jaipur 526,396
5 rows × 4 columns
Dialect Syntax for "first 5 rows"
SQL Server SELECT TOP 5 … ORDER BY … (also TOP 10 PERCENT, TOP 5 WITH TIES)
SQL Server 2012+, ANSI ORDER BY … OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 5 ROWS ONLY (Lesson 11)
PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, DuckDB … ORDER BY … LIMIT 5
Oracle FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY
Watch outTOP without ORDER BY

Without ORDER BY, the database returns rows in no guaranteed order, so "top 5" may differ between runs. Always sort when you use TOP.

WHERE: filtering rows

Comparison operators

SQL
SELECT COUNT(*) AS lines_over_50k
FROM superstore
WHERE sales > 50000;
Result
lines_over_50k
1126
1 rows × 1 columns
SQL
SELECT order_id, city, category, sales, discount
FROM superstore
WHERE region = 'West'
  AND category = 'Furniture'
  AND discount >= 0.3
ORDER BY sales DESC;
Result
order_id city category sales discount
IN-2025-02904 Ahmedabad Furniture 76,048 0.3
IN-2025-02783 Pune Furniture 69,762 0.3
IN-2024-01002 Indore Furniture 58,135 0.3
IN-2023-00431 Ahmedabad Furniture 54,474 0.3
IN-2025-02016 Ahmedabad Furniture 54,138 0.3
IN-2024-01490 Indore Furniture 49,728 0.3
139 rows × 5 columns (first 6 shown)

Text values go in single quotes ('West'). Double quotes are for identifiers in standard SQL. Dates are written as text in ISO format: order_date >= '2025-01-01'.

IN and NOT IN

IN is shorthand for several OR conditions on the same column.

SQL
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS order_lines
FROM superstore
WHERE city IN ('Pune', 'Mumbai', 'Ahmedabad')
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY city;
Result
city order_lines
Ahmedabad 373
Mumbai 283
Pune 529
3 rows × 2 columns
SQL
SELECT COUNT(*) AS non_metro_lines
FROM superstore
WHERE city NOT IN ('Delhi', 'Mumbai', 'Bengaluru', 'Chennai', 'Kolkata', 'Hyderabad');
Result
non_metro_lines
3918
1 rows × 1 columns
Common mistakesNOT IN with a NULL

If the list (or subquery) inside NOT IN contains a NULL, NOT IN returns no rows at all, because x <> NULL is UNKNOWN. Use NOT EXISTS (Lesson 10) or filter NULLs out of the subquery.

BETWEEN

BETWEEN a AND b is inclusive of both ends.

SQL
SELECT COUNT(*) AS lines_between_10k_and_20k
FROM superstore
WHERE sales BETWEEN 10000 AND 20000;
Result
lines_between_10k_and_20k
896
1 rows × 1 columns

For dates, prefer a half-open range: order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-01-01'. It works whether the column is DATE or DATETIME2; BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31' silently misses orders placed after midnight on 31-Dec when the column has times.

SQL
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders_in_2025
FROM superstore
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-01-01';
Result
orders_in_2025
1232
1 rows × 1 columns

LIKE: pattern matching

Wildcard Meaning Example Matches
% Any sequence of characters (including none) 'Apex%' Apex Chair 412, Apex Phone 118
_ Exactly one character 'C00_1' C0011, C0021 …
[ ] (SQL Server) One character from a set or range '[A-C]%' starts with A, B or C
[^ ] (SQL Server) One character not in the set '[^A-M]%' starts with N–Z
SQL
SELECT DISTINCT product_name
FROM superstore
WHERE product_name LIKE 'Apex Ch%'
ORDER BY product_name;
Result
product_name
Apex Chair 969
1 rows × 1 columns
SQL
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers_named_with_khan
FROM superstore
WHERE customer_name LIKE '%Khan%';
Result
customers_named_with_khan
44
1 rows × 1 columns
SQL
SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM superstore
WHERE city NOT LIKE '%a%'          -- city names without a lowercase 'a'
ORDER BY city;
Result
city
Delhi
Indore
Kochi
Lucknow
Pune
5 rows × 1 columns
NoteCase sensitivity

SQL Server's default collation is case-insensitive, so LIKE 'apex%' also matches "Apex…". PostgreSQL is case-sensitive (use ILIKE), and so is the practice engine used for the outputs in this handbook. Write patterns in the same case as the data to be safe everywhere.

Leading wildcards ('%Khan') cannot use an index and scan the whole table; fine for analysis, slow for apps on big tables.

IS NULL and IS NOT NULL

SQL
SELECT COUNT(*) AS homes_missing_area
FROM houses
WHERE area_sqft IS NULL;
Result
homes_missing_area
25

(The houses table is loaded from house_prices.csv; 25 houses have a missing area, which you will clean in the Python track.)

SQL
SELECT order_id, region, category, ship_mode, sales, profit
FROM superstore
WHERE (region = 'North' OR region = 'East')
  AND category <> 'Office Supplies'
  AND ship_mode IN ('First Class', 'Same Day')
  AND profit < 0
ORDER BY profit;

ORDER BY: sorting

SQL
SELECT region, city, COUNT(*) AS lines, ROUND(SUM(sales), 0) AS sales
FROM superstore
GROUP BY region, city
ORDER BY region ASC, sales DESC;
Result
region city lines sales
East Kolkata 430 13,888,466
East Patna 375 12,444,393
East Bhubaneswar 383 10,482,685
East Guwahati 335 9,668,576
North Delhi 453 15,657,610
North Chandigarh 361 11,541,792
North Lucknow 422 11,328,882
North Jaipur 294 10,489,878
16 rows × 4 columns (first 8 shown)
  • ASC (default) or DESC for each column separately.
  • Sort by an expression or alias: ORDER BY sales - profit DESC, ORDER BY margin_pct.
  • Sort by column position (ORDER BY 2 DESC) works but is fragile; avoid it in saved code.
  • NULLs sort first in ascending order in SQL Server (last in PostgreSQL/Oracle by default).
  • Custom order with CASE: ORDER BY CASE ship_mode WHEN 'Same Day' THEN 1 WHEN 'First Class' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END.

The logical processing order

You write SELECT first, but SQL processes the clauses in a different order. This explains several common errors.

Consequences:

  • You cannot use a column alias in WHERE, because WHERE runs before SELECT: WHERE margin_pct > 10 fails. Repeat the expression, or use a subquery/CTE.
  • You can use an alias in ORDER BY, because it runs after SELECT.
  • WHERE cannot contain aggregate functions (WHERE SUM(sales) > 100); use HAVING (Lesson 7).
SQL
-- Fails: Invalid column name 'margin_pct'
SELECT order_id, 100.0 * profit / sales AS margin_pct
FROM superstore
WHERE margin_pct > 10;

-- Works: repeat the expression in WHERE, use the alias in ORDER BY
SELECT order_id, 100.0 * profit / sales AS margin_pct
FROM superstore
WHERE 100.0 * profit / sales > 10
ORDER BY margin_pct DESC;

From business question to query

Step by stepTranslate a question

Question: "Which Technology orders in the South had a discount but still made more than ₹10,000 profit in 2025? Show the biggest first." 1. Table: superstore. 2. Rows (WHERE): category = Technology, region = South, discount > 0, profit > 10000, order date in 2025. 3. Columns (SELECT): order_id, order_date, city, sub_category, discount, profit. 4. Order: profit descending.

SQL
SELECT order_id, order_date, city, sub_category, discount, profit
FROM superstore
WHERE category = 'Technology'
  AND region = 'South'
  AND discount > 0
  AND profit > 10000
  AND order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY profit DESC;

Give an assistant your table's column list and a question, and ask for SQL Server syntax: "Table superstore(order_id, order_date, region, city, category, sub_category, sales, discount, profit). Summary

Key takeaways
  • SELECT columns and expressions; name them with AS; avoid SELECT * in saved queries.
  • DISTINCT removes duplicate rows of the selected columns; TOP n with ORDER BY limits results.
  • Filter with =, <>, >, <, >=, <=, AND/OR/NOT (use brackets), IN, BETWEEN (inclusive), LIKE with % and _, and IS NULL.
  • For dates use half-open ranges: >= start AND < next_start.
  • ORDER BY sorts ascending by default; can use aliases.
  • Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → TOP. That is why aliases fail in WHERE.
Quick quiz6 questions · tap an answer to check it

1. Which query returns each distinct region exactly once?

Answer: B. DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result.

2. WHERE sales BETWEEN 100 AND 200 includes which values?

Answer: B. BETWEEN is inclusive of both boundaries.

3. Which pattern finds product names that contain "Desk" anywhere?

Answer: C. % on both sides matches any characters before and after.

4. Why does WHERE margin_pct > 10 fail when margin_pct is an alias defined in SELECT?

Answer: A. Logical order: WHERE comes before SELECT.

5. What is wrong with WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31' on a DATETIME2 column?

Answer: B. '2025-12-31' means midnight; later times that day are excluded. Use < '2026-01-01'.

6. SELECT TOP 3 * FROM orders without ORDER BY returns:

Answer: C. Without ORDER BY, row order is not defined.
ExerciseSuperstore filters

Write queries for: (1) all Same Day orders in the West with sales over ₹50,000; (2) customers whose names start with A, B or C (distinct, sorted); (3) order lines with a 40% discount in the Furniture category, showing the 10 biggest losses; (4) the number of order lines in 2024 for the Corporate segment in Pune or Indore.

Show solution
SQL
-- (1)
SELECT order_id, order_date, city, sales FROM superstore
WHERE ship_mode = 'Same Day' AND region = 'West' AND sales > 50000 ORDER BY sales DESC;
-- (2) SQL Server
SELECT DISTINCT customer_name FROM superstore WHERE customer_name LIKE '[A-C]%' ORDER BY customer_name;
-- (3)
SELECT TOP 10 order_id, product_name, sales, profit FROM superstore
WHERE discount = 0.4 AND category = 'Furniture' ORDER BY profit ASC;
-- (4)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS lines FROM superstore
WHERE segment = 'Corporate' AND city IN ('Pune', 'Indore')
  AND order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01';
Interview cornerQuestions you may be asked

Q: What is the order of execution of a SQL query? FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, then TOP/OFFSET-FETCH.

Q: Difference between WHERE and HAVING? WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

Q: How do you find employees whose name's second letter is "a"? WHERE name LIKE '_a%'.

Q: IN vs EXISTS? IN compares a value with a list or subquery result; EXISTS checks whether a correlated subquery returns any row. EXISTS is safer with NULLs and often efficient for large subqueries (Lesson 10).

SQL for Data Analysis · Lesson 6

SQL Functions: Aggregate, Text, Date & Number

Use SQL Server's built-in functions to summarise, clean and reshape data. Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, STRING_AGG), text functions (LEN, LEFT, RIGHT, SUBSTRING, CHARINDEX, REPLACE, TRIM, UPPER, CONCAT), date functions (GETDATE, YEAR, MONTH, DATEPART, DATENAME, DATEADD, DATEDIFF, EOMONTH) and number functions (ROUND, CEILING, FLOOR, ABS, POWER, SQRT), plus CAST and CONVERT.

● SQL class 4✦ SQL Server 2022, 2026Beginner–Intermediate⏱ 120 min
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Distinguish scalar functions (one value per row) from aggregate functions (one value per group)
  • Summarise data with COUNT(*), COUNT(column), COUNT(DISTINCT), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and STRING_AGG
  • Clean and extract text with LEN, LEFT, RIGHT, SUBSTRING, CHARINDEX, REPLACE, TRIM, UPPER, LOWER and CONCAT
  • Work with dates using YEAR, MONTH, DATEPART, DATENAME, DATEADD, DATEDIFF, EOMONTH and DATEFROMPARTS
  • Round and convert numbers with ROUND, CEILING, FLOOR, ABS, POWER, SQRT, CAST, CONVERT and TRY_CAST

Two kinds of functions

Aggregate functions

Function Returns NULL handling
COUNT(*) Number of rows Counts every row
COUNT(col) Number of non-NULL values Skips NULLs
COUNT(DISTINCT col) Number of distinct non-NULL values Skips NULLs
SUM(col) Total Skips NULLs
AVG(col) Average of non-NULL values Skips NULLs (they are not treated as 0)
MIN(col), MAX(col) Smallest / largest (numbers, text, dates) Skips NULLs
STDEV(col), VAR(col) Sample standard deviation / variance Skips NULLs
STRING_AGG(col, sep) Values joined into one string Skips NULLs
SQL
SELECT COUNT(*)                         AS order_lines,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)         AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)      AS customers,
       ROUND(SUM(sales), 0)             AS total_sales,
       ROUND(AVG(sales), 0)             AS avg_line_sales,
       MIN(order_date)                  AS first_order,
       MAX(order_date)                  AS last_order,
       ROUND(STDEV(sales), 0)           AS sd_sales
FROM superstore;
Result
order_lines orders customers total_sales avg_line_sales first_order last_order sd_sales
6323 3200 785 201,413,569 31,854 2023-01-01 2025-12-31 60,414
1 rows × 8 columns
SQL
SELECT category,
       STRING_AGG(sub_category, ', ') AS sub_categories
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category, sub_category FROM superstore) AS t
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;
Result
category sub_categories
Furniture Bookcases, Chairs, Tables, Furnishings
Office Supplies Appliances, Art, Binders, Storage, Paper
Technology Phones, Machines, Copiers, Accessories
3 rows × 2 columns

In SQL Server add WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY sub_category) after STRING_AGG(...) to control the order of the joined values.

Watch outAVG of integers

AVG on an INT column returns an integer in SQL Server (AVG of 1, 2 = 1). Use AVG(quantity * 1.0) or AVG(CAST(quantity AS DECIMAL(10,2))) for decimals.

Text (string) functions

Function Example Result
LEN(s) LEN('Pune ') 4 (trailing spaces not counted)
UPPER(s), LOWER(s) UPPER('pune') PUNE
LEFT(s, n), RIGHT(s, n) LEFT('IN-2025-00042', 2) IN
SUBSTRING(s, start, n) SUBSTRING('IN-2025-00042', 4, 4) 2025
CHARINDEX(find, s) CHARINDEX('-', 'IN-2025-00042') 3
REPLACE(s, old, new) REPLACE('2025-04-27', '-', '/') 2025/04/27
TRIM(s), LTRIM, RTRIM TRIM(' Delhi ') Delhi
CONCAT(a, b, …) CONCAT(city, ', ', state) Pune, Maharashtra
REVERSE(s) REVERSE('abc') cba
REPLICATE(s, n) REPLICATE('*', 3) ***
STRING_SPLIT(s, sep) SELECT value FROM STRING_SPLIT('a,b,c', ',') 3 rows
FORMAT(value, fmt) FORMAT(1234567, 'N0', 'en-IN') 12,34,567
SQL
SELECT TOP 6
       order_id,
       LEFT(order_id, 2)                                   AS country,
       SUBSTRING(order_id, 4, 4)                           AS order_year,
       RIGHT(order_id, 5)                                  AS order_no,
       product_name,
       LEFT(product_name, CHARINDEX(' ', product_name) - 1) AS brand,
       UPPER(city)                                         AS city_upper,
       LEN(customer_name)                                  AS name_length
FROM superstore
ORDER BY row_id;
Result
order_id country order_year order_no product_name brand city_upper name_length
IN-2023-00001 IN 2023 00001 Nova Phone 223 Nova BENGALURU 12
IN-2023-00001 IN 2023 00001 Orbit Appliance 798 Orbit BENGALURU 12
IN-2023-00001 IN 2023 00001 Orbit Table 248 Orbit BENGALURU 12
IN-2023-00002 IN 2023 00002 Crest Storage 946 Crest AHMEDABAD 11
IN-2023-00003 IN 2023 00003 Crest Bookcase 170 Crest AHMEDABAD 10
IN-2023-00003 IN 2023 00003 Zenith Table 111 Zenith AHMEDABAD 10
6 rows × 8 columns

The brand is everything before the first space: CHARINDEX(' ', product_name) finds the space position, and LEFT(…, position − 1) cuts there. This is the SQL version of Excel's LEFT(A2, FIND(" ", A2) - 1) from Excel Lesson 5.

Cleaning text

SQL
WITH raw AS (
    SELECT '  bengaluru ' AS city UNION ALL
    SELECT 'BENGALURU'          UNION ALL
    SELECT 'Bangalore'          UNION ALL
    SELECT 'Bengaluru'
)
SELECT city                                                          AS raw_value,
       CONCAT(UPPER(LEFT(TRIM(city), 1)), LOWER(SUBSTRING(TRIM(city), 2, 100))) AS proper_case,
       CASE WHEN LOWER(TRIM(city)) IN ('bangalore', 'bengaluru') THEN 'Bengaluru' ELSE TRIM(city) END AS standardised
FROM raw;
Result
raw_value proper_case standardised
bengaluru Bengaluru Bengaluru
BENGALURU Bengaluru Bengaluru
Bangalore Bangalore Bengaluru
Bengaluru Bengaluru Bengaluru
4 rows × 3 columns

(SQL Server has no PROPER function; joining UPPER(LEFT(…,1)) and LOWER(SUBSTRING(…,2,…)) capitalises the first letter of a single word. Standardising spellings is best done with CASE or a mapping table joined in.)

Note`+` vs CONCAT for text

In SQL Server 'a' + 'b' joins text, but 'a' + NULL is NULL and 'Q' + 2 fails (it tries to convert 'Q' to a number). CONCAT('Q', 2) gives Q2 and treats NULL as empty. Prefer CONCAT.

Date and time functions

Function Example (d = '2026-04-27') Result
GETDATE(), SYSDATETIME() Current date and time
CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE) Today's date
YEAR(d), MONTH(d), DAY(d) MONTH(d) 4

DATENAME(part, d) DATENAME(month, d), DATENAME(weekday, d) April, Monday

FORMAT(d, 'MMM-yyyy') Apr-2026

Date parts you can use: year, quarter, month, dayofyear, day, week, weekday, hour, minute, second.

SQL
SELECT TOP 6
       order_id,
       order_date,
       ship_date,
       YEAR(order_date)                      AS yr,
       DATEPART(quarter, order_date)         AS qtr,
       DATENAME(month, order_date)           AS month_name,
       DATENAME(weekday, order_date)         AS weekday_name,
       DATEDIFF(day, order_date, ship_date)  AS days_to_ship,
       EOMONTH(order_date)                   AS month_end
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_date DESC;
Result
order_id order_date ship_date yr qtr month_name weekday_name days_to_ship month_end
IN-2025-03197 2025-12-31 2026-01-04 2025 4 December Wednesday 4 2025-12-31
IN-2025-03198 2025-12-31 2026-01-04 2025 4 December Wednesday 4 2025-12-31
IN-2025-03199 2025-12-31 2026-01-02 2025 4 December Wednesday 2 2025-12-31
IN-2025-03200 2025-12-31 2026-01-06 2025 4 December Wednesday 6 2025-12-31
IN-2025-03194 2025-12-30 2026-01-03 2025 4 December Tuesday 4 2025-12-31
IN-2025-03195 2025-12-30 2026-01-06 2025 4 December Tuesday 7 2025-12-31
6 rows × 9 columns
SQL
SELECT ship_mode,
       COUNT(*)                                         AS orders,
       AVG(DATEDIFF(day, order_date, ship_date) * 1.0)  AS avg_days_to_ship,
       MAX(DATEDIFF(day, order_date, ship_date))        AS max_days
FROM orders
GROUP BY ship_mode
ORDER BY avg_days_to_ship;
Result
ship_mode orders avg_days_to_ship max_days
Same Day 176 0.00 0
First Class 467 1.53 2
Second Class 621 3.00 4
Standard Class 1936 5.54 7
4 rows × 4 columns
Watch outDATEDIFF counts boundaries

DATEDIFF(year, '2025-12-31', '2026-01-01') returns 1, because one year boundary is crossed, even though only one day passed. For exact age use DATEDIFF(day, …)/365.25 or compare month and day as well.

Useful date patterns

SQL
-- Orders in the last 30 days
WHERE order_date >= DATEADD(day, -30, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE))

-- First day of the month
SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(order_date), MONTH(order_date), 1)   -- or DATETRUNC(month, order_date)

-- Indian financial year (April–March)
SELECT CASE WHEN MONTH(order_date) >= 4 THEN YEAR(order_date) + 1 ELSE YEAR(order_date) END AS fy

-- Month label for reports
SELECT FORMAT(order_date, 'MMM-yyyy') AS month_label
